articles.title: A new home for Fershman
articles.dek: The journal has a faster site, a members portal and a cleaner way to publish. Here's what changed, and the standards that haven't.
articles.body:
Fershman started with a simple bet: that students who read filings, model deals and argue about rates can write analysis worth reading. This site is built around that bet. It puts the argument first, keeps the evidence close behind it, and gets everything else out of the way.

## What's new

Every story now opens with its headline, a one-sentence standfirst and a clear byline. Data-heavy pieces can lead with **key figures** — the two or three numbers an argument turns on — so readers see the stakes before the first paragraph. Long reads get the full-width Big Read treatment on the front page.

> A good financial story is an argument with a number attached. Lead with both.

Members also have a private portal for the decks, models and recordings we use internally, organized by meeting and searchable in one place. Readers can get every new story by email.

## How a story gets made

The standards haven't changed. Every piece still moves through the same stages:

| Stage | Who | Typical time |
|---|---|---|
| Pitch | Writer | 1 day |
| Draft | Writer | 5–10 days |
| Edit | Section editor | 2–4 days |
| Publish | Editors | Same day |

Writers draft and submit their work for review in the new admin panel. Section editors edit, schedule and publish it.[^1]

## Write for us

If you've spotted something the market is mispricing, or a parallel from history that everyone is missing, [send us a pitch](/submit). Six hundred words of original thinking beat two thousand words of summary.

[^1]: Times are typical, not guaranteed. Longer investigations take longer.

articles.title: A price is a message, not a sticker
articles.dek: Why prices rise when something gets scarce, and what that tells everyone who never sees the shortage.
articles.body:
Imagine a frost wipes out a third of the orange crop. Most people who buy orange juice will never hear about it. Yet within weeks, they buy less of it. Nobody told them to. The price did.

## What the price is doing

A price coordinates people who will never meet. When supply falls, the same buyers now compete for fewer oranges. Sellers can charge more and still sell out, so they do. The higher price then does three jobs at once:

- **It rations.** Buyers who value juice least switch to something else, so what's left goes to the people who value it most.
- **It signals.** Growers elsewhere see unusually high prices and plant more, or release more from storage.
- **It rewards.** Growers who protected their trees earn more, which pays them back for the precaution.

## A quick model

Economists draw this with two curves. Demand slopes down: the higher the price, the less people want. Supply slopes up: the higher the price, the more producers are willing to sell. The market price sits where the curves cross.

A frost shifts the supply curve to the left — at every price, fewer oranges are for sale. The new crossing point has a **higher price and a lower quantity**. No one planned that outcome. It emerged from millions of separate choices.

> Capping the price doesn't make oranges less scarce. It only hides the message.

## Why it matters

If a government caps the price of juice at the old level, the shortage doesn't go away. Buyers still want the old amount, growers have less to sell, and shelves empty. The scarcity is still there; it's paid for in time spent queuing instead of money.

**The takeaway:** a price is information about scarcity, compressed into a single number. Read it that way and much of economics becomes intuitive.

articles.title: What a bond yield is really telling you
articles.dek: Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions. Here's why, with one table of arithmetic.
articles.body:
A bond is a promise: pay me $1,000 today, and I'll pay you $40 a year for ten years, then give your $1,000 back. That $40 is the **coupon** — 4% of the face value — and it never changes.

## The one idea

The coupon is fixed, but the return the market demands is not. If newly issued bonds start paying 5%, nobody will pay full price for your old 4% bond. To sell it, you have to cut the price until the buyer earns 5% anyway. That required return is the **yield**.

So the price does all the adjusting:

- When yields **rise**, existing bond prices **fall**.
- When yields **fall**, existing bond prices **rise**.

## The arithmetic

A bond's price is the value today of every payment it will make, each discounted at the market yield. For our ten-year bond with a 4% coupon, that gives:

| Market yield | Bond price | Change vs. face value |
|---|---|---|
| 3% | $1,085.30 | +8.5% |
| 4% | $1,000.00 | 0.0% |
| 5% | $922.78 | −7.7% |
| 6% | $852.80 | −14.7% |

A one-point move in yields shifts this bond's price by roughly 8%. That sensitivity is called **duration**,[^1] and it's why long-term bonds swing more than short-term ones.

## Reading the market

When you see a headline like "Treasury yields jump," translate it: bond prices just fell, borrowing just got more expensive, and investors now want more to lend for that long. Mortgage rates, corporate loans and stock valuations all key off that number. Short-term yields, in turn, follow the Federal Reserve's policy rate closely:

**The takeaway:** yields and prices are two ways of quoting the same thing. Learn to flip between them, and every rate headline becomes readable.
